questions.stem: What must two atoms share to be isotopes of the same element?

options.explanation: Proton count fixes the element; isotopes differ only in neutrons.
Differing neutrons is exactly what makes them isotopes.
Mass numbers differ between isotopes.

options.text: the same number of electrons and neutrons
options.explanation: Neutrons differ; electrons are irrelevant to the definition.

questions.stem: How do chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 differ?

options.explanation: Shared proton count means the same element.
35 − 17 = 18 and 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons: a difference of two.
Both have 17 protons — extra protons would change the element.
Neutral atoms of both have 17 electrons.

questions.stem: An isotope’s mass number differs from another isotope of the same element because…

options.explanation: Electron loss changes charge, not the mass number.
Nuclear size is not what the mass number measures.

options.text: its nucleus holds a different number of neutrons
options.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons; only neutrons vary.

options.text: its nucleus holds a different number of protons
options.explanation: Protons are constant across isotopes.

questions.stem: Which pair of numbers could describe two isotopes of the same element?

options.explanation: Different atomic numbers are different elements.

options.text: atomic number 8, mass numbers 16 and 17 protons
options.explanation: A proton change would alter the atomic number.
Again two elements, not isotopes.
Shared atomic number with different mass numbers is the isotope pattern.

questions.stem: Why are isotopes of an element chemically indistinguishable in most reactions?

options.text: because chemistry depends on electrons, and their count tracks the unchanged proton number
options.explanation: Equal protons give equal electrons in neutral atoms, so chemistry matches.
Their masses differ — that is the definition.
Neutrons are chemically inert inside the nucleus.

options.text: because isotopes always decay at the same rate
options.explanation: Decay behaviour differs between isotopes.

questions.modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

questions.stem: State what stays the same and what changes between two isotopes of carbon.
questions.modelAnswer: The proton count stays the same (6 for carbon) while the neutron count changes, so the mass number changes too.

questions.stem: Explain why an atom with 8 protons and 10 neutrons is an isotope of oxygen rather than a different element.
questions.modelAnswer: The proton count of 8 fixes the element as oxygen; the neutron count only selects which isotope of oxygen it is.

questions.stem: Two neutral atoms have notations of atomic number 17 with mass numbers 35 and 37. Give the neutron and electron counts for each atom.
questions.modelAnswer: Each atom has 17 protons and 17 electrons; the neutrons are 35 − 17 = 18 and 37 − 17 = 20 respectively.

questions.stem: What makes some isotopes more unstable than others?

options.explanation: Stability is nuclear, not chemical.

options.text: an imbalance between their protons and neutrons
options.explanation: The proton-neutron balance governs nuclear stability.
Electrons do not affect nuclear stability.
Nuclear stability is not set by atomic size.

questions.stem: Which isotope of hydrogen is rarer, deuterium or tritium?

options.explanation: The abundances differ by many orders of magnitude.
Both occur naturally, in the stated tiny fractions.
Tritium is about 1 in a billion billion; deuterium is 2 in 10,000.
Deuterium is far more common than tritium.

questions.stem: About 2 in every 10,000 hydrogen atoms are deuterium. What fraction is that?

options.explanation: That would be 20 in 10,000 — ten times too high.
That would be 0.2 in 10,000 — ten times too low.
That magnitude belongs to tritium, not deuterium.
2/10,000 simplifies to 1/5,000.

questions.stem: Why might an unstable isotope be unlikely to occur naturally in large amounts?

options.text: because unstable nuclei decay away over time
options.explanation: Decay converts the isotope into other nuclei, depleting natural stores.

options.text: because it is too chemically reactive to form compounds
options.explanation: The scarcity is nuclear, not chemical.

options.text: because it cannot exist on Earth
options.explanation: Unstable isotopes exist; they simply do not persist.
Decay changes identity, not the argument about abundance.

questions.stem: Two isotopes of an element have very different proton-neutron ratios. What else will differ?

options.text: their electron configuration in neutral atoms
options.explanation: Equal protons mean equal electrons and similar chemistry.
Stability, set by the ratio, sets the decay likelihood.

options.text: their position in the periodic table
options.explanation: Both share the same atomic number and so the same position.
The element symbol is shared.

questions.stem: Name the two heavier isotopes of hydrogen and state how many neutrons each contains.
questions.modelAnswer: Deuterium is hydrogen with one neutron, and tritium is hydrogen with two neutrons.

questions.stem: State the approximate natural abundance of deuterium among hydrogen atoms.
questions.modelAnswer: Deuterium makes up about 2 in every 10,000 hydrogen atoms.

questions.stem: Explain why an isotope with a large proton-neutron imbalance may be less likely to occur naturally.
questions.modelAnswer: The imbalance makes the nucleus unstable, so it decays into other nuclei; over time the unstable isotope is depleted and becomes rare in nature.

questions.stem: A sample contains 100,000 hydrogen atoms. Estimate how many are deuterium, and name the rarer isotope.
questions.modelAnswer: At 2 in 10,000, the sample holds about 20 deuterium atoms; tritium is the rarer isotope.
